title: Welded joints: butt and fillet welds and the throat stress

explain.say: Ships, bridges, car chassis and cranes are held together by welds: metal melted and fused into one piece. Look at the two main kinds. A butt weld joins plates edge to edge; a fillet weld fills the corner where plates meet, like a triangular bead.

explain.say: A fillet weld breaks along its weakest plane: the throat, the shortest line from the corner to the face of the triangle. For an equal-leg fillet, the throat is 0.707 times the leg, because the triangle has 45 degree angles. Why do you think 0.707 appears?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Fillet welds are the most common in machines

explain.say: It is one over root two, the cosine of 45 degrees. Now a worked example. A bracket carries 50 kilonewtons on two 100 millimetre fillet welds with 6 millimetre legs. Throat area is 0.707 times 6 times 200: about 848 square millimetres. Shear stress is 50,000 over 848, about 59 megapascals.

explain.say: At 3 millimetres the stress doubles to 118, still under 145, so yes for static load. Brilliant! But welds have a hidden weakness: the heat-affected zone and the weld toe are stress raisers, so welds under repeated loads need much lower stresses. Exam tip: weld length counts only where the weld is full size.

faq.q: What is the difference between butt and fillet welds?
faq.a: A butt weld joins parts edge to edge, usually in a prepared groove, and can be as strong as the plate. A fillet weld is a triangular bead in a corner or lap joint, and its strength depends on its throat.

faq.q: How do I calculate the strength of a fillet weld?
faq.a: Divide the load by the throat area: 0.707 times leg size times weld length. Compare that shear stress with the allowable stress for the electrode.

faq.q: What is the allowable stress for a weld?
faq.a: A common rule for fillet welds under static load allows about 0.3 times the electrode tensile strength in shear, about 145 megapascals for a 482 megapascal electrode. Design codes set the exact value.

faq.q: What is the throat of a weld?
faq.a: The shortest distance from the root of a fillet weld to its face. For an equal-leg fillet it is 0.707 times the leg length, and it is where failure usually happens.

faq.q: Why are welds weak in fatigue?
faq.a: The weld toe has a sharp change of shape, and welding leaves residual stresses and small defects, so cracks start there easily under repeated loads.

facts: The throat of an equal-leg fillet weld is 0.707 times its leg length.
Welded joints usually have much lower fatigue strength than the plain parent metal.
